column1: First three commands for any broken pod?
column2: kubectl get pods -o wide; kubectl describe pod X (read EVENTS); kubectl logs X --previous

column1: What does `kubectl get endpoints <svc>` tell you?
column2: Whether the Service selector matches any pods. No endpoints = selector problem. This bisects most Service issues instantly.

column1: requests vs limits?
column2: request = what the SCHEDULER reserves (decides placement). limit = what the KERNEL cgroup enforces. CPU is throttled; memory is killed.

column1: The three QoS classes?
column2: Guaranteed (requests==limits everywhere), Burstable (requests<limits), BestEffort (neither). BestEffort is evicted first.

column1: Difference between liveness and readiness probes?
column2: Liveness failure RESTARTS the container. Readiness failure removes it from Service endpoints without restarting.

column1: Why should a liveness probe never check a database?
column2: A DB blip fails liveness on every pod simultaneously, restarting the whole fleet and turning a blip into an outage. Dependency checks belong in readiness.

column1: What is a startupProbe for?
column2: Slow-starting apps. It suppresses liveness and readiness until it passes, so a slow boot isn't killed.

column1: Pod is Pending - where do you look?
column2: kubectl describe pod, the FailedScheduling event. It names the reason verbatim: insufficient cpu/memory, untolerated taint, unbound PVC, node affinity.

column1: Scheduling is based on what - requests or usage?
column2: Requests. A cluster at 10% actual CPU can be 100% unschedulable if requests are overset.

column1: ReadWriteOnce vs ReadWriteMany?
column2: RWO = one node at a time (EBS, block storage). RWX = many nodes (EFS/NFS). Scaling a Deployment with an RWO volume across nodes fails.

column1: Why would a PVC stay Pending and that be correct?
column2: volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer - it waits for a pod so the volume is created in the right AZ.

column1: ClusterRole bound with a RoleBinding - what is the scope?
column2: Only that one namespace. This is legal and often intended but surprises people.

column1: What apiGroup do core resources like pods use?
column2: The empty string "". Deployments use "apps".

column1: pods/log and pods/exec in RBAC?
column2: Separate sub-resources. Granting "pods" does not grant log or exec.

column1: How do you check permissions for a service account?
column2: kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:ns:name -n target

column1: Why do pods hang in Terminating when a node dies?
column2: The control plane cannot confirm the containers are gone. Force-deleting risks split-brain double-writes - data corruption for a StatefulSet.

column1: What is IRSA?
column2: IAM Roles for Service Accounts. A projected service account token is exchanged via the cluster OIDC provider for temporary AWS credentials. No keys on disk.

column1: Default bridge vs user-defined Docker network?
column2: User-defined networks have embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11 that resolves container names. The default bridge does not. This is why Compose "just works".

column1: NetworkPolicy with default-deny egress breaks everything. Why?
column2: It blocks DNS to CoreDNS on port 53, so every name lookup fails. Always pair default-deny with an explicit DNS allow rule.

column1: Do NetworkPolicies work with any CNI?
column2: No. Calico and Cilium enforce them. Flannel does not - the policy applies and silently does nothing.

column1: What is a PodDisruptionBudget for?
column2: Limits how many pods can be voluntarily disrupted at once (drains, upgrades). Prevents a node drain from taking down a whole service.

column1: kubectl imperative YAML generation?
column2: kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > d.yaml
